title: Agent Loop & Tool Use
scopeHtml: Scope: The agent loop, function calling, tool design and termination.

notes.title: What an agent is
notes.html:
Definition. An agent is a system in which an LLM repeatedly decides the next action, uses tools to act on the world or fetch information, observes the results, and continues until a goal is achieved or a stop condition triggers. The defining feature is that the model directs the control flow, not the programmer.

Workflow vs agent.

Workflow (orchestration in code) Agent (control flow by the model)
Path predefined steps and branches chosen dynamically
Predictability high lower; non-deterministic
Debugging standard logging needs trace/transcript tooling
Cost/latency bounded variable, can balloon
Best for known, repeatable procedures open-ended tasks with unpredictable steps

Escalation ladder. Start with a single LLM call (with good prompt and retrieval). Move to a workflow (prompt chaining, routing, parallelization, orchestrator-workers, evaluator-optimizer) when one call is insufficient but the steps are knowable. Use a true agent only when the path can't be enumerated in advance and the value justifies the cost and risk.

Typical agent components.

  1. Model (planner/decider).
  2. Tools (functions, APIs, code interpreter, browser, database, file system).
  3. Instructions (system prompt: goal, rules, tool-use guidance).
  4. Memory/state (conversation, scratchpad, long-term store).
  5. Control loop and stop conditions (code).
  6. Guardrails and permissions (code).
  7. Observability (traces).

Real life. A fixed assembly line (workflow) versus a handyman told "fix the leak" who decides what to try (agent).

Interview angle. The standard question: "when would you use an agent instead of a workflow?" Answer with predictability, error cost, and enumerability.

notes.title: The loop
notes.html:
Core algorithm.

messages = [system, user_goal]
for step in range(MAX_STEPS):
    reply = llm(messages, tools=TOOLS)
    messages.append(reply)
    if not reply.tool_calls:
        return reply.text                      # final answer
    for call in reply.tool_calls:              # execute in code, never by the model
        result = run_tool(call.name, call.args)   # validate, authorize, timeout, catch errors
        messages.append(tool_result(call.id, result))
    if budget_exceeded() or no_progress(messages):
        return fail_safely()
raise MaxStepsExceeded

Rules that make it correct.

  • The model proposes calls; your code executes them after validation and authorization.
  • Every tool call receives a matching result (or an error result) before the next model call.
  • Keep the entire assistant turn (text + tool calls) in history in the format the API requires.
  • The model is stateless: each iteration resends the history.

Stop conditions (all in code).

  • Model returns a final answer (no more tool calls).
  • Max iterations/tool calls.
  • Token/cost budget and wall-clock timeout.
  • Success predicate (tests pass, goal state reached).
  • No-progress detection (same call repeated, same error N times).
  • Human interrupt or approval denial.
  • Safety triggers.

Common loop bugs. No max steps (runaway), dropping tool results, forgetting to append the assistant message, swallowing errors silently, retrying non-idempotent actions, ignoring the finish reason (truncated output mid tool call).

Real life. A detective alternating between thinking and checking evidence, working to a deadline.

notes.title: Designing tools
notes.html:
Tool quality drives agent quality. Treat tool definitions as the agent's user interface: design for a model reader.

Guidelines.

  1. Specific names (get_order_status, not get_data).
  2. Descriptions that route: what it does, when to use it, when not to, what it returns, limits, formats. Include examples for non-obvious parameters.
  3. Narrow, composable operations over a giant do-everything tool; but also avoid dozens of near-duplicate tools.
  4. Minimal required parameters; sensible defaults; enums for closed sets; ISO formats; validate on the server.
  5. Return concise, relevant, structured output: trim, paginate, summarize big payloads, include ids needed for follow-up calls; avoid dumping 50 KB JSON into context.
  6. Meaningful errors: say what went wrong and how to fix it ("end_date must be after start_date").
  7. Idempotency and safety: read vs write tools clearly separated; destructive tools require explicit confirmation parameters or approval; use idempotency keys for retries.
  8. Least privilege: each tool gets the minimal scopes; per-user credentials, never shared superuser keys.
  9. Namespacing and grouping for large tool sets; load tools on demand (tool search) to avoid overloading context.
  10. Test tools like APIs: unit tests, schema tests, and agent-level evals of tool selection.

Anti-patterns. Overlapping tools with similar descriptions; tools requiring knowledge the model can't have (internal ids with no lookup tool); ambiguous parameters; returning raw HTML/huge logs; hidden side effects in "read" tools.

Real life. A well-labelled toolbox beats a drawer of unlabelled gadgets.

notes.title: Tool errors and recovery
notes.html:
Error taxonomy.

  • Invalid arguments (model's fault): return a clear validation error so it can fix and retry.
  • Not found / empty result: return an explicit "no results" message, not a blank; the model should try broader queries or ask.
  • Permission denied: terminal; do not retry; tell the model to inform the user.
  • Transient (timeout, 429, 5xx): retry in code with backoff and jitter; the model often need not see these unless retries fail.
  • Partial failure: report which parts succeeded.
  • Unsafe/blocked by policy: return a refusal reason.

Principles.

  1. Never return an empty success on failure. The model treats silence as valid data and continues with false premises.
  2. Flag errors explicitly (e.g. is_error: true plus a message); keep messages actionable and free of secrets.
  3. Bound retries (per call and per run); detect repeated identical failures and break out or escalate.
  4. Make write operations idempotent so retries don't duplicate effects.
  5. Surface unrecoverable errors to the user with a clear explanation and the state reached.
  6. Log everything with correlation ids.

Real life. A mechanic told "the part is out of stock" can order another; one told nothing assumes it was fitted.

notes.title: Parallel and sequential calls
notes.html:
Parallel calls. When subtasks are independent (look up three customers, fetch two documents), the model can emit multiple tool calls in one turn; your code executes them concurrently and returns all results together. Benefits: lower latency, fewer model turns.

Sequential calls. When one call needs another's output (find user id → fetch orders), they occur across turns.

Implementation points.

  • Return one result per call id, in the format required; order isn't important but ids must match.
  • Cap concurrency (provider rate limits, downstream capacity).
  • Handle partial failures: some succeed, some fail.
  • Avoid parallelizing calls with side effects that conflict (two writes to the same record) — serialize or lock.
  • Some APIs let you disable parallel tool use when determinism is preferred.

Design for dependency. Tools should expose what's needed to decide parallelism: independent lookups as separate read-only tools; batch tools (get_orders(ids=[...])) when many ids are needed.

Real life. Ordering starters for the table together, but you can't plate dessert before the main is eaten.

notes.title: Context in agent loops
notes.html:
Why context is the bottleneck. Each iteration resends the whole history. Tool results are appended and remain. A run with 30 steps and 3k-token results accumulates ~90k tokens; cost per step rises, latency rises, and quality can degrade (context rot) or the window overflows. Agents often fail around "turn N" for exactly this reason.

Techniques.

  • Trim tool outputs at the source (return only needed fields, paginate).
  • Offload large artifacts (files, long documents) to storage and pass references; let the agent read parts on demand.
  • Clear or summarize stale tool results once used (keep decisions and key facts).
  • Compaction: periodically summarize the conversation preserving task state, decisions, file paths, errors and resolutions.
  • Sub-agents with isolated context for exploration; they return concise summaries.
  • Scratchpad/notes file for persistent plans and facts outside the window.
  • Prompt caching for stable prefix (system prompt, tool definitions).
  • Budgets: token counters, early warnings, graceful wrap-up.

Symptom check. If tool selection or instruction following gets worse after a fixed number of steps, check context size first.

Real life. A desk so cluttered you lose the original brief; keep only the working papers and file the rest.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
Definition. An agent is an LLM in a tool-using loop that chooses its own path; workflows script the path. Prefer single call → workflow → agent, escalating only as needed.

Loop. Model proposes tool calls; code validates, authorizes and executes; results returned for every call; history resent each turn. Always define stop conditions in code: max steps, budgets, timeouts, success predicates, no-progress detection, human interrupts.

Tool design. Specific names, routing descriptions (when and when not), minimal required parameters, enums, concise structured outputs, actionable errors, idempotency, least privilege, few distinct tools, tested like APIs.

Errors. Return explicit error results (never empty success); classify transient vs terminal; bounded retries with backoff; detect repeated failures; surface unrecoverable errors.

Parallelism. Independent calls in parallel with concurrency caps and per-id results; dependent calls sequential; serialize conflicting writes.

Context management. Trim outputs, offload artifacts, clear/summarize stale results, compact, use sub-agents and notes, cache static prefixes, set budgets; degradation after N steps usually means context bloat.

Interview one-liners.

  • "The model proposes, the code disposes: execution and policy live outside the model."
  • "Tool descriptions are prompts; say when not to use the tool."
  • "An empty result on failure is the most dangerous bug in an agent."
  • "Agents fail by context bloat before they fail by capability."

questions.promptHtml: What is an "agent" in the LLM sense, and how is it different from a workflow that also calls an LLM?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: "Agent" is an overloaded buzzword. The signal is whether you can say precisely who controls the flow, and what that costs.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: An LLM is a text-prediction model. An agent is an LLM placed in a loop where it can call tools (functions that read data or take actions), see the results, and decide the next step until the goal is met. The key difference from a workflow is who owns the control flow. In a workflow, my code fixes the steps ("summarize, then classify, then email"). In an agent, the model chooses the steps at runtime. Agents are more flexible but less predictable, slower, and costlier.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Plain-words glossary first. A tool is a function you describe to the model (name, purpose, parameters); the model can ask you to run it. A loop means we call the model, run whatever it asked for, feed the results back, and call it again. Control flow means "what happens next".

Workflow:  code -> LLM(step1) -> code -> LLM(step2) -> code -> LLM(step3) -> done
           (path is written by the developer, same every time)

Agent:     goal -> LLM -> tool? -> result -> LLM -> tool? -> result -> LLM -> answer
           (path is chosen by the model, differs per run)
Workflow Agent
Path predefined dynamic
Predictability high lower, non-deterministic
Debugging normal logs needs traces of whole transcript
Cost/latency bounded variable, can balloon
Best for known repeatable procedure open-ended tasks, unknown number of steps

Typical agent parts: model, tools, instructions (system prompt), memory/state, the control loop with stop conditions, guardrails/permissions, and observability (traces). Notice that four of these seven are ordinary code. The "agent" is a software system around a model, not the model alone.

Runtime behavior: every iteration is a fresh stateless API call that re-sends the full history. The model has no memory except what you resend.

sections.label: Code
sections.html: Not needed for this definitional question; the loop itself is shown in the next questions.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Calling any app that makes an LLM call an agent. A fixed chain of prompts is a workflow.
  • Thinking the model executes tools itself. It only emits a request; your code runs it.
  • Treating "agentic" as strictly better. It is a trade of predictability for flexibility.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Is a router (LLM picks one of 3 branches, then code runs it) an agent? → No, that is a workflow with an LLM-made decision; there is no loop of observe-then-decide.
  2. What is the biggest new failure mode agents add? → Unbounded or looping behavior and compounding errors across steps.
  3. How do you test something non-deterministic? → Evaluate on task-level success over many runs, plus unit tests for tools, plus trace review.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "an LLM that can use tools." Senior: "an LLM that directs its own control flow in a loop; I choose it only when the path cannot be enumerated in advance and the value justifies variable cost and risk."

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team shipped an "agent" that always did the same four steps; it was really a workflow, and rewriting it as one cut latency by half and removed random failures.

questions.promptHtml: Walk me through the agent loop step by step. What does the model do, and what does your code do?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: If you cannot draw this loop and state who does what, you cannot debug any agent framework.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: I send the model the goal plus a list of tool definitions. The model replies with either a final answer or one or more tool-call requests. My code validates and runs those tools, appends the results to the conversation, and calls the model again. This repeats until the model answers without tool calls or a stop condition I coded triggers, such as a max step count. The model proposes, my code executes.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Terms: a message is one entry in the conversation (system, user, assistant, tool result). A tool call is a structured request such as {id: "t1", name: "get_order", args: {order_id: 42}}. The tool result is the output your code sends back, tagged with the same id.

Steps:

  1. Build messages = [user goal] and call the model with the tool list.
  2. Append the model's whole reply (text and tool calls) to history, exactly as the API format requires.
  3. If there are no tool calls, return the text. Done.
  4. Otherwise, for each call: validate arguments, check permission, run with a timeout, catch errors, and append a result for that call id.
  5. Check budgets and progress, then go to step 1.

Correctness rules: every call gets a matching result (even if it is an error), the full assistant turn stays in history, and the model is stateless so history is re-sent every time. With the Anthropic API, a tool call arrives as a tool_use content block (the response stop_reason is "tool_use"), and the result goes back in a user message as a tool_result block with the matching tool_use_id. OpenAI-style APIs use a tool role message with tool_call_id.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
def run_agent(goal, llm, tools, max_steps=15):
    messages = [{"role": "user", "content": goal}]
    for _ in range(max_steps):
        reply = llm(messages)              # {"text": str, "tool_calls": [{"id","name","args"}]}
        messages.append({"role": "assistant", "reply": reply})
        if not reply["tool_calls"]:
            return reply["text"]
        for c in reply["tool_calls"]:
            try:
                out = tools[c["name"]](**c["args"])
            except Exception as e:         # never crash the loop on a tool error
                out = f"ERROR: {e}"
            messages.append({"role": "tool", "id": c["id"], "content": str(out)})
    raise RuntimeError("max steps exceeded")
// Llm is a placeholder interface; wire it to your SDK (Anthropic Java SDK, Spring AI, LangChain4j).
data class Call(val id: String, val name: String, val args: Map<String, Any>)
data class Reply(val text: String, val calls: List<Call>)
fun interface Llm { fun chat(history: List<Any>): Reply }

fun runAgent(goal: String, llm: Llm, tools: Map<String, (Map<String, Any>) -> String>, maxSteps: Int = 15): String {
    val history = mutableListOf<Any>(goal)
    repeat(maxSteps) {
        val reply = llm.chat(history)
        history += reply
        if (reply.calls.isEmpty()) return reply.text
        for (c in reply.calls) {
            val out = try { tools.getValue(c.name)(c.args) } catch (e: Exception) { "ERROR: ${e.message}" }
            history += mapOf("tool_call_id" to c.id, "content" to out)
        }
    }
    error("max steps exceeded")
}
// Llm is a placeholder interface; wire it to your SDK.
record Call(String id, String name, Map<String, Object> args) {}
record Reply(String text, List<Call> calls) {}
interface Llm { Reply chat(List<Object> history); }

static String runAgent(String goal, Llm llm, Map<String, Function<Map<String, Object>, String>> tools, int maxSteps) {
    List<Object> history = new ArrayList<>(List.of(goal));
    for (int i = 0; i < maxSteps; i++) {
        Reply reply = llm.chat(history);
        history.add(reply);
        if (reply.calls().isEmpty()) return reply.text();
        for (Call c : reply.calls()) {
            String out;
            try { out = tools.get(c.name()).apply(c.args()); }
            catch (Exception e) { out = "ERROR: " + e.getMessage(); }
            history.add(Map.of("tool_call_id", c.id(), "content", out));
        }
    }
    throw new IllegalStateException("max steps exceeded");
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Forgetting to append the assistant message before the tool results (the API rejects or the model loses its own request).
  • Running the tool inside the model call path with no try/catch, so one exception kills the whole run.
  • No step cap.
  • Assuming the model remembers earlier calls without history being re-sent.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why re-send the whole history? → The API is stateless; context is the only memory.
  2. What if the model calls a tool that does not exist? → Return an error result listing valid tool names; do not crash.
  3. How does this change with streaming? → You must accumulate partial tool-call JSON until the block completes before executing.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: describes think-act-observe. Senior: states the invariants (matching ids, full assistant turn kept, code-owned execution and stop conditions) and the failure modes when one is violated.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A hand-rolled loop that skipped appending the assistant turn produced intermittent 400 errors from the API only when the model made two tool calls in one turn.

questions.promptHtml: What does a tool definition look like, and how does the model "call" a function it cannot run?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests whether you understand function calling as structured output plus a contract, not remote code execution.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A tool definition has a name, a plain-language description, and a JSON Schema for the parameters. The provider shows this to the model along with the prompt. If the model decides a tool is useful, it emits a structured request with the tool name and JSON arguments. It never runs anything. My code parses that, runs the real function, and sends back the result. The description is effectively a prompt, so how well I write it decides whether the model picks the right tool.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
JSON Schema is a standard way to describe the shape of JSON (types, required fields, allowed values). The model is trained to produce JSON that fits the schema, but fitting the schema is not a guarantee of valid business values, so I always re-validate on my side.

Example definition (Anthropic format uses input_schema; OpenAI uses parameters inside a function object):

Flow: prompt + tool list -> model decides -> tool_use {name, input} -> code runs -> tool_result -> model continues.

What can go wrong: the model hallucinates an argument (an invented order id), picks a wrong tool when descriptions overlap, or omits a required field. Defenses: enums for closed sets, clear parameter descriptions with examples, server-side validation, and error messages the model can act on.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
get_order = {
    "name": "get_order_status",
    "description": "Look up the status of ONE customer order by its numeric id. "
                   "Use when the user asks where their order is. Do not use for refunds.",
    "input_schema": {
        "type": "object",
        "properties": {"order_id": {"type": "integer", "description": "e.g. 10482"}},
        "required": ["order_id"],
    },
}
# client.messages.create(model="claude-sonnet-5-5", max_tokens=1024, tools=[get_order], messages=[...])
// The same schema as plain maps; serialize to JSON with your library (Jackson, kotlinx.serialization).
val getOrder = mapOf(
    "name" to "get_order_status",
    "description" to "Look up the status of ONE customer order by numeric id. Not for refunds.",
    "input_schema" to mapOf(
        "type" to "object",
        "properties" to mapOf("order_id" to mapOf("type" to "integer", "description" to "e.g. 10482")),
        "required" to listOf("order_id"),
    ),
)
// The Anthropic Java SDK also has typed builders for tools; verify exact class names in the SDK docs.
Map<String, Object> getOrder = Map.of(
    "name", "get_order_status",
    "description", "Look up the status of ONE customer order by numeric id. Not for refunds.",
    "input_schema", Map.of(
        "type", "object",
        "properties", Map.of("order_id", Map.of("type", "integer", "description", "e.g. 10482")),
        "required", List.of("order_id")));
// Typed tool builders exist in com.anthropic:anthropic-java; verify exact names in the SDK docs.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Believing the model executes the function.
  • Trusting the arguments without validation because "the schema was enforced".
  • Vague descriptions like "gets data".
  • Putting secrets or user-specific ids the model should not control into the model-controlled arguments.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Is strict schema adherence guaranteed? → Not by default; some providers offer strict/structured modes, but business validation is still mine.
  2. Where do tool definitions count? → They consume input tokens on every call; many tools get expensive.
  3. Can the model call a tool with no arguments? → Yes, with an empty object schema.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "give the model a function signature." Senior: "the description is a routing prompt, the schema is a contract I still re-validate, and authorization is derived from the session, not from model arguments."

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A tool accepted user_id from the model; a prompt injection made it query another customer's data. Moving user_id to the server-side session closed it.

questions.promptHtml: How does an agent loop end? List the stop conditions you would build and where each one lives.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Runaway loops are the classic first production incident. The right answer puts the stops in code, not in the prompt.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: The happy path ends when the model answers without any tool call. But I never rely on that alone. In code I add a max step count, a token or cost budget, a wall-clock timeout, a success check where one exists (tests pass, record created), no-progress detection (same call or same error repeating), a human interrupt or approval denial, and safety triggers. A prompt saying "stop after 10 steps" is a hint, not a guarantee.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Why code and not prompt: the model can ignore, forget or never reach an instruction; a counter in your loop cannot. Each stop returns a deliberate outcome: a partial result with an explanation, an escalation to a human, or a clean failure, never a silent hang.

Stop Protects against Typical value
Max steps runaway loops 10-30 for task agents
Token/cost budget bill shock per-run dollar cap
Wall clock stuck tools, user waiting 60-300 s
Success predicate doing extra work tests green
No progress repeated identical failures same call 3 times
Human gate risky actions approval required

Graceful wrap-up: when the budget is at about 80 percent, inject a message telling the model to summarize what is done and what remains, so the final stop yields value instead of a dead end.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
import time
def budget_ok(step, tokens, started, max_steps=20, max_tokens=200_000, max_secs=120):
    return step < max_steps and tokens < max_tokens and time.time() - started < max_secs
fun budgetOk(step: Int, tokens: Int, startedMs: Long,
             maxSteps: Int = 20, maxTokens: Int = 200_000, maxMs: Long = 120_000) =
    step < maxSteps && tokens < maxTokens && System.currentTimeMillis() - startedMs < maxMs
static boolean budgetOk(int step, int tokens, long startedMs) {
    return step < 20 && tokens < 200_000 && System.currentTimeMillis() - startedMs < 120_000;
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Only a max step cap, with no cost or time cap (20 steps at 100k tokens each is still expensive).
  • Throwing an exception at the cap with no partial result for the user.
  • Counting steps but not tool retries inside a step.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What do you return when the cap hits? → The best partial result, what was done, what remains, and a flag so the UI can offer to continue.
  2. How do you pick the cap? → From traces: take the p95 of successful runs and add headroom.
  3. Why a token budget? → Cost per step grows as history grows, so step counts alone understate spend.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "set max iterations." Senior: layers several independent stops, designs the graceful exit, and tunes limits from trace percentiles.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An agent with only a prompt-level "do not exceed 10 searches" instruction looped 400 times on a flaky search tool.

questions.promptHtml: A PM wants "an AI agent" for a feature. How do you decide between a single LLM call, a workflow, and a true agent?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Seniors prevent over-engineering. The signal is a principled escalation ladder with cost and risk reasoning.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: I start with the simplest thing that could work: one LLM call with a good prompt and retrieved context. If one call is not enough but I can write down the steps, I use a workflow (prompt chaining, routing, parallelization, orchestrator-workers, evaluator-optimizer). I only use a true agent when I cannot enumerate the path ahead of time and the task value justifies variable cost and the risk of mistakes. Three questions drive it: can the steps be listed, what does a wrong action cost, and what latency and cost can the user bear?

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Decision aids:

  • Enumerability: "refund an order" has four known steps, so use a workflow. "Find why the checkout service errors" has unknown steps, so use an agent.
  • Error cost: sending an email or moving money argues for fixed steps with approval gates; reading and summarizing tolerates agent freedom.
  • Verifiability: if a success check exists (tests, schema, a record), agents are safer because loops can self-correct against it.
  • Latency and cost: an agent with 12 steps at 4 seconds each is nearly a minute; users of a chat widget will leave.

Hybrid is normal: a workflow whose one node is a bounded agent (for example, the "investigate" step has an agent with a 10-step cap, the rest is deterministic). Component accounting: more autonomy means more guardrails, traces, evals, and incident cost.

sections.label: Code
sections.html: Not needed; it is a design decision.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Picking an agent because the demo looked impressive.
  • Ignoring that reliability compounds: 10 steps at 95 percent each is about 60 percent end to end (0.95^10 = 0.599).
  • Not budgeting for evals and observability that agents need.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What is evaluator-optimizer? → One LLM call generates, another critiques, and the loop repeats under a cap; it is a workflow because the structure is fixed.
  2. When is a workflow with an LLM router enough? → When there are a handful of known intents, each with a fixed handler.
  3. How do you migrate from workflow to agent safely? → Make one step agentic with a cap and a fallback to the old path, compare on evals.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "agents for complex tasks." Senior: gives the ladder, quantifies compounding error and latency, and proposes bounded hybrids.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A support bot rebuilt from a free-roaming agent to a router plus three fixed flows saw resolution rate rise and cost per ticket drop by about 60 percent (illustrative).

questions.promptHtml: What makes a good tool name, description and parameter set for an LLM, as opposed to for a human developer?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tool quality drives agent quality. Interviewers want to see that you treat tool definitions as a user interface for a model.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: The model only sees the name, description and schema, so those are its entire understanding of the tool. I use specific names like get_order_status not get_data. The description says what it does, when to use it, when not to, what it returns and limits. I keep required parameters minimal, use enums for closed sets, give examples for non-obvious formats, and return short structured output with ids for follow-up calls. The test is: could a new hire pick the right tool from this text alone?

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Think of the definition as part of the system prompt. Typical failures come from ambiguity:

  • Two tools both say "search documents": the model flips a coin.
  • A parameter date with no format: the model sends "yesterday".
  • A tool needs an internal customer_uuid the model cannot know, with no lookup tool: it hallucinates one.

Guidelines:

  1. Narrow composable operations, but not 40 near-duplicates.
  2. Negative guidance ("not for refunds, use create_refund").
  3. Constrain input: enums, ISO-8601 dates, numeric ranges, minLength.
  4. Output design: include only needed fields, paginate, summarize big payloads, never dump 50 KB of JSON or raw HTML into the context.
  5. Actionable errors ("end_date must be after start_date").
  6. Separate read tools from write tools; no hidden side effects in a "get".

Testing: write unit tests for the tool like an API, plus an eval that measures tool selection accuracy over 50 to 200 realistic prompts.

questions.contextHtml:
You inherit this loop. About 1 in 15 runs fails with a provider error: "tool_use ids were found without tool_result blocks immediately after" (HTTP 400). It only happens on requests where the model asked for two tools at once. Logs show both tools executed fine. The team suspects a flaky provider.

def run(goal, tools):
    messages = [{"role": "user", "content": goal}]
    while True:
        resp = client.messages.create(model="claude-sonnet-5-5", max_tokens=1024,
                                      tools=TOOLS, messages=messages)
        if resp.stop_reason != "tool_use":
            return resp.content[0].text
        for block in resp.content:
            if block.type == "tool_use":
                out = tools[block.name](**block.input)
                messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": resp.content})
                messages.append({"role": "user", "content": [
                    {"type": "tool_result", "tool_use_id": block.id, "content": str(out)}]})
questions.promptHtml: Find every bug and explain the 400.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add retries for the provider error." It treats a deterministic client-side protocol violation as flakiness and misses the other bugs.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Does the failure correlate with multiple tool_use blocks (yes, per the logs)? Any max step cap (no, it is while True)? Are tools ever slow or raising? These tell me whether the bug is protocol-level.
  2. Immediate mitigation: Add a step cap now so a bad run cannot spin, and ship the structural fix below behind a fast deploy.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) assistant message and tool results are appended inside the per-block loop, so with two tool calls the assistant message appears twice and results arrive in separate user messages; (b) no try/except, so one tool exception crashes the run; (c) while True has no cap; (d) resp.content[0].text may not be text if the final block order differs.
  4. How I'd verify each: Log the serialized messages for a failing run. I expect assistant, user(result 1), assistant, user(result 2). The API requires all tool_result blocks for one assistant turn in the single next user message.
  5. Root cause: The protocol says every tool_use id in an assistant turn must have its tool_result in the immediately following user message. My loop splits them and also duplicates the assistant turn.
  6. Fix: Append the assistant turn once, collect all results, append one user message.
  7. Prevention: A unit test with a fake model that returns two tool calls; a lint on message shape (every tool_use id has a result); a step cap; error results instead of exceptions.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not retries (deterministic failure), not "just disable parallel tool use" as the only fix (it hides the bug and loses latency benefits, though it is a valid short-term mitigation).
def run(goal, tools, max_steps=15):
    messages = [{"role": "user", "content": goal}]
    for _ in range(max_steps):
        resp = client.messages.create(model="claude-sonnet-5-5", max_tokens=1024,
                                      tools=TOOLS, messages=messages)
        messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": resp.content})
        if resp.stop_reason != "tool_use":
            return "".join(b.text for b in resp.content if b.type == "text")
        results = []
        for b in resp.content:
            if b.type == "tool_use":
                try:
                    out, err = str(tools[b.name](**b.input)), False
                except Exception as e:
                    out, err = f"{type(e).__name__}: {e}", True
                results.append({"type": "tool_result", "tool_use_id": b.id,
                                "content": out, "is_error": err})
        messages.append({"role": "user", "content": results})
    raise RuntimeError("max steps")
// Shape of the fix with placeholder types: one assistant entry, then ONE user entry holding all results.
for (step in 0 until maxSteps) {
    val resp = llm.chat(history)
    history += Assistant(resp.blocks)                       // once per turn
    val calls = resp.blocks.filterIsInstance<ToolUse>()
    if (calls.isEmpty()) return resp.text()
    history += UserResults(calls.map { c ->
        runCatching { ToolResult(c.id, tools.getValue(c.name)(c.input), isError = false) }
            .getOrElse { ToolResult(c.id, "${it::class.simpleName}: ${it.message}", isError = true) }
    })                                                      // once per turn, all ids present
}
for (int step = 0; step < maxSteps; step++) {
    Resp resp = llm.chat(history);
    history.add(new Assistant(resp.blocks()));              // once per turn
    List<ToolUse> calls = resp.blocks().stream()
        .filter(b -> b instanceof ToolUse).map(b -> (ToolUse) b).toList();
    if (calls.isEmpty()) return resp.text();
    List<ToolResult> results = new ArrayList<>();
    for (ToolUse c : calls) {
        try { results.add(new ToolResult(c.id(), tools.get(c.name()).apply(c.input()), false)); }
        catch (Exception e) { results.add(new ToolResult(c.id(), e.toString(), true)); }
    }
    history.add(new UserResults(results));                  // once per turn, all ids present
}

  • What if the final turn is truncated at max_tokens mid tool call? → Check stop_reason == "max_tokens" separately; do not execute partial arguments.
  • Can results be in any order? → Order inside the results message is flexible, ids must match and results must come first in that user message (verify in provider docs).

questions.promptHtml: A tool fails. How do you decide whether the model should see the error, whether to retry, and what to put in the message?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Error handling separates demo agents from reliable ones. They want a taxonomy and a policy, not "try/except".

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: I classify the failure. Invalid arguments are the model's fault, so I return a clear validation error so it can fix and retry. Empty results get an explicit "no results found" message. Permission denied is terminal: no retry, tell the user. Transient errors (timeout, 429, 5xx) I retry in code with exponential backoff and jitter, and the model only sees them if retries fail. Partial failures report what succeeded. And I never return an empty success on failure.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Terms: transient = likely to succeed if tried again soon. Terminal = retrying cannot help. Backoff = wait longer between tries (for example 0.5 s, 1 s, 2 s). Jitter = add randomness so many clients do not retry at the same instant.

Class Who handles Action
Invalid args model return is_error with the exact fix
Not found / empty model explicit "0 results", suggest broader query
Permission denied user stop, explain, no retry
Transient code bounded retry, backoff + jitter
Partial model list ok and failed parts
Policy block model refusal reason

Principles: error text must be actionable and secret-free (no stack traces with connection strings); bound retries per call (3) and per run; detect the same error repeating; log with a correlation id; make writes idempotent so retries are safe.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
import random, time
TRANSIENT = (TimeoutError, ConnectionError)
def call_with_retry(fn, tries=3, base=0.5):
    for i in range(tries):
        try:
            return fn()
        except TRANSIENT:
            if i == tries - 1:
                raise
            time.sleep(base * 2 ** i + random.uniform(0, base))
suspend fun <T> callWithRetry(tries: Int = 3, baseMs: Long = 500, fn: suspend () -> T): T {
    repeat(tries - 1) { i ->
        try { return fn() } catch (e: java.io.IOException) {
            kotlinx.coroutines.delay(baseMs * (1L shl i) + (0..baseMs).random())
        }
    }
    return fn() // last attempt; let the exception propagate
}
static <T> T callWithRetry(Callable<T> fn, int tries, long baseMs) throws Exception {
    for (int i = 0; i < tries; i++) {
        try { return fn.call(); }
        catch (IOException e) {
            if (i == tries - 1) throw e;
            Thread.sleep(baseMs * (1L << i) + ThreadLocalRandom.current().nextLong(baseMs));
        }
    }
    throw new IllegalStateException();
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Returning "" or [] on failure.
  • Retrying permission errors or validation errors.
  • Retrying non-idempotent writes.
  • Leaking stack traces or secrets into the model context.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why hide transient errors from the model? → Cheaper and avoids the model improvising workarounds for a blip.
  2. How to stop an infinite retry between model and tool? → Count identical failures per run; escalate after N.
  3. 429 with Retry-After header? → Honor it over your own backoff.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "catch exceptions and return the message." Senior: classifies, retries only what is safe, bounds everything, and treats silent empty returns as the worst bug.

questions.contextHtml: A support agent answers "where is my order?" using get_order_status(order_id). Over a weekend, 1,900 of 12,000 conversations (16 percent) told customers "your order has not shipped yet". Support then received 340 angry tickets about orders that had shipped days earlier. No errors appear in the agent logs and latency is normal at 2.1 s p50. A deploy on Friday rotated the warehouse API credentials. Model and prompts were unchanged.
questions.promptHtml: What happened, how do you confirm it, and how do you prevent a repeat?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "The model hallucinated; tune the prompt." It never inspects the tool output and keeps the root cause in place.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What did the tool return for a failing order (raw payload)? Does the rate align with the Friday deploy? Do the logs record tool outputs or only model text? Is the 16 percent uniform or concentrated on certain warehouses? These separate model error from data error.
  2. Immediate mitigation: Disable the order tool path or route to "let me connect you to a human", and send corrections to the 1,900 affected users.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) the tool swallows a 401 and returns an empty or default object that reads as "no shipment yet"; (b) the warehouse API partially degraded; (c) prompt change (ruled out); (d) model drift (unlikely given the sharp onset).
  4. How I'd verify each: Replay 20 failed conversation ids and print the exact tool result. Query the warehouse API with the new credentials in a shell. Check HTTP status distribution in the tool's own logs by hour.
  5. Root cause: The tool code wrapped the HTTP call in except Exception: return {"shipments": []}. A 401 became an empty list, which the model correctly interpreted as "nothing shipped".
  6. Fix: Return an explicit error result for non-2xx and distinguish "order exists, no shipments" from "lookup failed".
  7. Prevention: Contract tests asserting failures raise; alert on tool error rate; dashboards of tool outputs by outcome class; canary conversations run every 5 minutes; a rule that tools never return success-shaped data on failure.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not prompt-level "be careful" (cannot fix missing data). Not retrying 401s.
def get_order_status(order_id: int) -> dict:
    r = http.get(f"{WH}/orders/{order_id}/shipments", timeout=5)
    if r.status_code == 404:
        return {"error": "order_not_found", "message": f"No order {order_id}"}
    if r.status_code in (401, 403):
        raise PermissionError("warehouse credentials rejected")   # surfaces as is_error to the model
    r.raise_for_status()
    return {"shipments": r.json()}
fun getOrderStatus(orderId: Int): Map<String, Any> {
    val r = http.get("$WH/orders/$orderId/shipments")
    return when (r.status) {
        404 -> mapOf("error" to "order_not_found", "message" to "No order $orderId")
        401, 403 -> throw SecurityException("warehouse credentials rejected")
        in 200..299 -> mapOf("shipments" to r.json())
        else -> throw IllegalStateException("warehouse HTTP ${r.status}")
    }
}
static Map<String, Object> getOrderStatus(int orderId) {
    var r = http.get(WH + "/orders/" + orderId + "/shipments");
    return switch (r.status()) {
        case 404 -> Map.of("error", "order_not_found", "message", "No order " + orderId);
        case 401, 403 -> throw new SecurityException("warehouse credentials rejected");
        default -> {
            if (r.status() / 100 != 2) throw new IllegalStateException("warehouse HTTP " + r.status());
            yield Map.of("shipments", r.json());
        }
    };
}

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if the API is eventually consistent and "no shipments" can be true for 10 minutes after paying? → Return {"shipments": [], "note": "shipment records can lag up to 10 min"} so the model hedges.
  • What if the tool is third-party and you cannot change it? → Wrap it in an adapter that normalizes errors.
  • How do you find the other silent tools? → Chaos test: break each dependency and assert the tool errors.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: Two weeks after the fix a second tool had the same except: return [] pattern; a grep for broad catches in tool modules found nine more.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Blames the model or prompt.
  • Hire: Inspects tool output, finds swallowed 401, returns explicit errors.
  • Strong hire: Distinguishes empty-vs-failed semantics, adds canaries and alerts, and audits all tools for the pattern.

questions.promptHtml: What are parallel tool calls, when are they safe, and how do you implement them correctly?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Latency and correctness both depend on this. Seniors know that parallelism is easy for reads and dangerous for writes.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: In one turn the model can request several tool calls at once if they are independent, for example looking up three customers. My code runs them concurrently and returns one result per call id in the next message. This cuts latency and model turns. Dependent calls (find user id, then fetch orders) are naturally sequential across turns. I cap concurrency, handle partial failures, and serialize or lock calls that write to the same resource.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Latency math: three 2 s lookups sequentially take 6 s plus three model turns; in parallel they take about 2 s plus one model turn.

turn 1: model -> [get_user(1), get_user(2), get_user(3)]
code:   run concurrently (cap 5) -> 3 results
turn 2: model -> final answer

Implementation points:

  • One tool_result per call id; order does not matter, ids must match.
  • Concurrency cap, because of provider rate limits and downstream capacity.
  • Partial failure: return successes and error results together; never drop a failed one.
  • Conflicting writes (two updates to the same record) must be serialized or locked.
  • Some APIs let you disable parallel tool use (Anthropic: disable_parallel_tool_use inside tool_choice; verify in docs) when determinism matters.
  • Design tools for it: independent read tools, and batch tools (get_orders(ids=[...])) when many ids are common.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor
def run_calls(calls, tools, max_workers=5):
    def one(c):
        try:
            return {"id": c["id"], "content": str(tools[c["name"]](**c["args"])), "is_error": False}
        except Exception as e:
            return {"id": c["id"], "content": f"{type(e).__name__}: {e}", "is_error": True}
    with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers) as ex:
        return list(ex.map(one, calls))   # ex.map preserves input order
suspend fun runCalls(calls: List<Call>, tools: Map<String, suspend (Map<String, Any>) -> String>): List<Result> =
    coroutineScope {
        val gate = kotlinx.coroutines.sync.Semaphore(5)          // concurrency cap
        calls.map { c -> async {
            gate.withPermit {
                runCatching { Result(c.id, tools.getValue(c.name)(c.args), false) }
                    .getOrElse { Result(c.id, "${it::class.simpleName}: ${it.message}", true) }
            }
        } }.awaitAll()
    }
static List<Result> runCalls(List<Call> calls, Map<String, Function<Map<String, Object>, String>> tools) {
    ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(5);      // concurrency cap
    try {
        List<Future<Result>> fs = calls.stream().map(c -> pool.submit(() -> {
            try { return new Result(c.id(), tools.get(c.name()).apply(c.args()), false); }
            catch (Exception e) { return new Result(c.id(), e.toString(), true); }
        })).toList();
        List<Result> out = new ArrayList<>();
        for (var f : fs) { try { out.add(f.get(30, TimeUnit.SECONDS)); } catch (Exception e) { /* map to error result with call id */ } }
        return out;
    } finally { pool.shutdown(); }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Parallelizing writes to the same record.
  • Losing the id mapping, or dropping a failed call's result.
  • No concurrency cap, causing 429 storms.
  • Assuming the model will always batch; it may emit calls one at a time.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does the model run the calls in parallel? → No, it only emits them in one turn; my code decides execution.
  2. When disable parallel use? → Strict ordering, conflicting writes, or deterministic replay.
  3. Batch tool vs parallel calls? → Batch is better when the backend can fetch many ids in one query.

sections.html: 3 YOE: "run them at the same time." Senior: caps concurrency, preserves id pairing, isolates failures, and serializes conflicting writes.

questions.promptHtml: Why do agents get slower, costlier and worse as a run gets longer, and what does it mean that "context is the bottleneck"?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Most long-run agent failures are context failures. They want mechanism plus numbers.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: The model is stateless, so every loop iteration re-sends the whole history, and each tool result stays in it. A context window is the maximum amount of text (measured in tokens) the model can read at once. A 30-step run with 3k-token results accumulates roughly 90k tokens of results alone, so per-step cost and latency climb, quality can degrade as the model has more irrelevant text to sift through, and eventually the window overflows. So I manage context actively.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Arithmetic: if step k carries about 3k * k tokens, total input tokens processed across 30 steps is about 3k * (1 + 2 + ... + 30) = 3k * 465 = roughly 1.4M tokens, not 90k. Cost grows roughly quadratically with step count unless cached or trimmed. Prompt caching (reusing the already-processed stable prefix of the prompt at a discount; verify provider specifics) softens this for the system prompt and tool definitions, but the growing tail is still billed.

Quality: long contexts dilute attention; instructions given early can get less weight ("context rot"). Symptom: tool selection or instruction following worsens after a fixed number of steps.

Techniques (detailed in a later question): trim outputs at source, offload large artifacts, clear stale results, compact via summaries, use sub-agents, keep a notes file, cache stable prefixes, set budgets.

sections.label: Code
sections.html: Not needed; see the dedicated context-management question for implementation.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Returning whole documents from tools.
  • Assuming a bigger window removes the problem; cost and quality effects remain.
  • Measuring only step count and not context size.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does caching fix it? → It reduces cost of the stable prefix, not the growth or the quality dilution.
  2. How do you measure it? → Log input tokens per step; plot against step number and against success.
  3. What is first to trim? → Old tool results that have already been consumed.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "the context window fills up." Senior: shows the quadratic cost, ties symptoms to step number, and has a ladder of mitigations.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An agent's success rate fell from 82 percent for runs under 15 steps to 41 percent for runs beyond 30; the trigger was context size, not task difficulty (illustrative).

On an eval of 120 questions, the correct tool is chosen 64 percent of the time. Confusions are concentrated between search_docs, search_wiki and find_files. Average run uses 6.8 tool calls versus 3.1 for a hand-routed baseline. Switching to a larger model improved accuracy only to 69 percent.
questions.promptHtml: How do you fix tool selection without changing the model?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Use a better model or add few-shot examples to the system prompt." The tools themselves are ambiguous; no model can resolve them.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What corpus does each tool actually cover? Are the three really different backends? Which user intents are most common? Do tools overlap in content? This tells me whether to merge or sharpen.
  2. Immediate mitigation: Add differentiating descriptions to the worst pair today; it is a config change.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) overlapping vague descriptions; (b) true functional overlap, so the split is artificial; (c) tools need ids or inputs the model cannot know; (d) too many tools (not here, only 4).
  4. How I'd verify each: Build a confusion matrix from the eval; read 20 failed traces; ask a teammate to choose tools from the descriptions alone (if humans are confused, the model will be).
  5. Root cause: Descriptions do not say what each source holds, when to use it, or when not to.
  6. Fix: Merge search_docs and search_wiki into search_knowledge(source: enum[docs, wiki, any]) if the backend allows; rewrite descriptions with scope, example queries and "not for" lines; return source labels in results.
  7. Prevention: Keep the tool-selection eval in CI; add a lint that rejects descriptions under a minimum length or sharing high similarity with another tool.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not one mega-tool with 15 parameters; not stuffing long routing rules in the system prompt that duplicate tool text.
